title: A theory purified of everything but law
subtitle: Kelsen's pure theory: the basic norm and the hierarchy of validity
objectives: State the core claim of Kelsen's pure theory: law as a self-contained system of norms, purified of sociological, political and moral content
Explain the basic norm (Grundnorm) as the presupposed foundation of a legal system's validity, and the Stufenbau hierarchy it supports
Contrast Kelsen's Grundnorm with Hart's rule of recognition, and identify where each account is most exposed to criticism

leadingAuthorities.citation: Kelsen, Pure Theory of Law (1934; rev. edn 1960, trans. 1967)
leadingAuthorities.role: Sets out the pure theory: a legal system as a hierarchy of norms, each deriving its validity from a norm above it, ultimately from a presupposed basic norm

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students routinely lump Kelsen in with Hart as 'the positivists' and stop there. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of understanding, this brief note appears: 'You can name the Grundnorm — this lesson checks whether you can say exactly how it differs from Hart's rule of recognition, and why that difference is contested.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans on scenarios — a coup succeeding or failing, a chain of norms to trace — rather than definitions alone.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take the is/ought distinction slowly — it's the hinge the whole pure theory turns on, and nothing later in the lesson makes sense without it.

overview.hook: Try to explain why a parking fine is legally binding without once mentioning whether the fine is fair, whether people actually pay it, or which political party wrote the rule. Hans Kelsen thought that was exactly the discipline legal theory needed — a theory of law with the sociology, the politics and the morality surgically removed, leaving only the question of validity itself. What's left, once you strip all that away, turns out to be a strange and demanding answer.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Kelsen's pure theory is long-settled historical scholarship, and the debate with Hart described here remains a live, unresolved fault line within positivism rather than a closed question — this lesson states both positions as contested, not as settled law.

parts.heading: The ambition of a 'pure' theory
parts.voice: expository — introduces Kelsen's founding move before complicating it
body: Kelsen was reacting against two rival ways of explaining law, and he wanted no part of either. One reduced law to sociology or psychology — what officials actually do, what people habitually obey, who holds power. The other grounded law's validity in morality — natural law's claim that an unjust rule isn't really law at all. Kelsen thought both approaches smuggled something non-legal into a question that ought to be answered on its own terms.

His method rests on a distinction borrowed from philosophy: the 'is' (Sein) and the 'ought' (Sollen). Facts about the world — what happened, what people do, who has the guns — belong to the realm of 'is'. Norms — what ought to be done — belong to a separate realm entirely, and Kelsen insisted you cannot validly derive an 'ought' from an 'is' alone. A norm's validity can only be explained by reference to another norm, never by reference to a bare social fact.

This is what 'pure' means in the pure theory: purified of sociology, purified of politics, purified of moral evaluation. The theory asks one question only — what makes a given norm legally valid within a system of norms — and refuses to answer it by pointing to obedience, efficiency, justice or anything else outside the normative system itself.

components.definition: Kelsen's account of law as a self-contained system of valid norms, deliberately purified of sociological, political and moral content. A norm's validity is explained only by reference to another, higher norm — never by social facts about obedience or power, and never by moral facts about justice.

interaction.prompt: On Kelsen's account, can a legal norm's validity ever be explained simply by the fact that people generally obey it?
options: No — validity is a normative question, answered only by reference to another norm
Yes — widespread obedience is itself sufficient to make a norm valid
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Obedience is a fact about the world (an 'is'); for Kelsen, validity is a question that can only be answered within the normative system itself (an 'ought').
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at the is/ought distinction — obedience is a sociological fact, and Kelsen's whole method is built on refusing to derive a norm's validity from a fact of that kind.

parts.heading: The basic norm: why the chain needs a first link
parts.voice: Socratic — builds the puzzle before resolving it
body: A parking regulation is valid because a local authority was empowered to make it by statute. The statute is valid because the constitution empowered Parliament to legislate. Push the question back one more step: what makes the constitution itself valid? You cannot answer with another positive legal norm, because that would only push the question back again — an infinite regress with no floor.

Kelsen's answer is the basic norm, or Grundnorm. It is not an enacted rule found in any statute book. It is a presupposed, hypothetical norm that legal science must assume in order to treat the historically first constitution — and everything validly created under it — as binding: roughly, 'one ought to behave as the first constitution prescribes.' It isn't legislated by anyone, and asking who enacted it is a category mistake.

The Grundnorm makes no moral claim that the constitution is just or good. It is a purely formal, logical precondition — the minimum you must presuppose before you can describe any system of norms as a valid legal order at all, rather than as a mere set of threats backed by force.

components.definition: The presupposed, unenacted norm that legal science must assume in order to treat a constitution — and the norms validly created under it — as legally binding. It is not itself validated by any higher norm; it is the necessary starting point of the whole hierarchy of validity.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that Kelsen treats the Grundnorm as an actual rule enacted by some identifiable legislative body?
interaction.explanation: Not enacted. The Grundnorm is deliberately not a posited legal rule — it is a presupposition legal science makes in order to treat the first constitution as binding, and asking 'who enacted the Grundnorm' misunderstands what kind of thing it is.

parts.heading: Stufenbau: law as a stepped hierarchy
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Kelsen — with the concept developed further by his collaborator Adolf Merkl — described a legal system as a Stufenbau: a 'stepped construction' in which every level of norms derives its validity from, and must conform to, the level immediately above it, terminating in the Grundnorm.

A typical hierarchy runs: the Grundnorm (presupposed) → the historically first constitution → general norms enacted under that constitution, such as statutes → further general norms made under delegated authority, such as regulations → individual norms that apply the general norms to a particular case, such as a judicial decision, an administrative order or a contract.

The crucial move is that each level is simultaneously application and creation. A judge deciding a case is not passively 'finding' law that already exists in full; the judgment is a new individual norm, authorised by — and subordinate to — the statute the judge applies. Validity flows downward through the hierarchy at the same moment new, more concrete norms are being created.

components.title: The Stufenbau: a stepped hierarchy of validity
components.description: Each level derives its validity from the level above it, ultimately from the presupposed Grundnorm.

nodes.label: General norms enacted under the constitution (statutes)
Further general norms made under delegated authority (regulations)
Individual norms applying general norms to a case (judgments, administrative acts, contracts)

components.textAlternative: The Grundnorm is presupposed as the foundation. It gives validity to the historically first constitution, which authorises general norms such as statutes, which in turn authorise further general norms such as regulations, which are applied to particular cases through individual norms such as judgments, administrative acts and contracts. Each level derives its validity from the one above it.

interaction.prompt: Order these from the most foundational to the most concrete in Kelsen's hierarchy.
items: A statute enacted under the constitution
A judge's decision applying the statute to a case
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the Stufenbau: validity flows downward from the presupposed Grundnorm, through the constitution and statute, to the individual judgment that applies them to a particular case.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the direction of validity, not the order of enactment in time — the Grundnorm sits beneath everything else, and the judge's decision is the most concrete, most downstream norm in the chain.

parts.heading: Revolution and the puzzle of a new Grundnorm
parts.voice: problem-posing — sets up a genuinely hard case before resolving it
body: Kelsen's theory has to explain legal change, including the hardest case: what happens, legally, when a coup or revolution succeeds and establishes a wholly new order, breaking continuity with the old constitution entirely?

His answer is that legal science must presuppose a new Grundnorm once — and only once — the new order becomes generally efficacious: actually obeyed and enforced as a matter of overall social fact. A coup that seizes a television station for a day and is then reversed never achieves this; its decrees are not law at all, however much force backed them, and the old Grundnorm remains presupposed throughout. A revolution that succeeds in establishing lasting, general compliance is different: at that point, legal science presupposes a new Grundnorm and reinterprets the new order as validly law.

This is one of the pure theory's most debated moves. Efficacy is a fact about the world — an 'is' — and critics have long pressed Kelsen on whether letting efficacy determine when a new Grundnorm may be presupposed really keeps validity as purely normative as the theory claims. Kelsen's defenders reply that efficacy is only a condition for presupposing the Grundnorm, not itself the source of validity — the Grundnorm, once presupposed, still does the normative work. The dispute has never been fully settled.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume the Grundnorm changes automatically at the moment a coup seizes power, simply because the old government has been physically displaced.
components.whyItsWrong: Physical displacement is not enough. On Kelsen's account, a new Grundnorm is presupposed only once the new order achieves general, lasting efficacy — actual widespread compliance — not at the moment force is first used.

interaction.prompt: In which scenario does Kelsen's theory support presupposing a new Grundnorm?
interaction.scenarioA: A faction seizes the national broadcaster and declares a new government; within 48 hours the army restores the previous administration, and the old courts, officials and public resume operating exactly as before.
interaction.scenarioB: A faction seizes power, and eighteen months later its decrees are being enforced nationwide, its courts are functioning, taxes are being collected under its authority, and no rival government exerts effective control anywhere in the territory.
interaction.explanation: B shows the general, lasting efficacy Kelsen's theory requires before legal science presupposes a new Grundnorm. A shows a failed attempt with no lasting efficacy — the old constitutional order, and its Grundnorm, remains presupposed throughout.

parts.heading: Kelsen against Hart: presupposition or social fact?
parts.voice: comparative — closes the lesson by locating the live disagreement
body: Kelsen and Hart are routinely grouped together as 'legal positivists', and they do share one core commitment: the separation of law from morality, and the search for an ultimate criterion that explains why a legal system's norms count as valid law at all. But their accounts of that ultimate criterion differ sharply — and the difference is exactly where each theory is most exposed.

Hart's rule of recognition, covered in Lesson 5, is an empirical, sociological fact about officials: it exists only if courts actually accept and apply certain criteria of validity in practice, from what Hart calls the internal point of view. In principle, you could go and observe whether a rule of recognition exists in a given system by watching what judges say and do.

Kelsen's Grundnorm is deliberately not that kind of fact. It is a presupposition of legal science — required to interpret norms as legally valid — not a description of anyone's actual beliefs or conduct. This is Kelsen's debt to Kant: a 'transcendental-logical' presupposition, not an empirical claim you could falsify by observation.

A committed Hartian would press Kelsen here: doesn't this make the Grundnorm suspiciously unfalsifiable and metaphysically thin, next to a rule of recognition you can actually point to in observable official practice? A committed Kelsenian would press back: doesn't Hart's grounding of validity in social fact readmit exactly the sociology the pure theory was built to exclude — and doesn't Kelsen's efficacy requirement for a new Grundnorm show Hart isn't wrong to think some fact has to do the work somewhere? Neither side has persuaded the other. This is a live fault line within positivism itself, not a settled question with a correct answer.

components.label: Grundnorm vs rule of recognition, at a glance
points: Grundnorm — a presupposed, unenacted norm; a logical precondition of treating a constitution as binding, not a description of anyone's actual practice
Rule of recognition — an empirical, sociological fact about what officials actually accept and use as criteria of validity, observable from the internal point of view
Both aim to answer the same question — what makes a legal system's norms ultimately valid — but locate the answer in different places: presupposition vs social practice
Each is vulnerable from the other's position: the Grundnorm risks being unfalsifiable; the rule of recognition risks readmitting the sociology Kelsen wanted excluded

interaction.prompt: Which statement best captures the core difference between Kelsen's Grundnorm and Hart's rule of recognition?
options: The Grundnorm is a moral standard the constitution must meet; the rule of recognition is a purely formal test
The Grundnorm is a presupposed logical precondition of validity; the rule of recognition is an empirical social fact about official practice
The two are simply different names for the same idea, restated in different vocabularies
interaction.trapExplanation: The first option gets it backwards — neither concept is a moral standard, since both Kelsen and Hart separate law from morality. The third option flattens a real and contested difference: one is presupposed by legal science, the other is an observable fact about what officials do.

testPool.prompt: In one sentence, state what Kelsen's basic norm (Grundnorm) is.
acceptableAnswers: the presupposed norm that makes the first constitution binding
a hypothetical presupposed norm underlying the validity of the legal system
the unenacted presupposition that the first constitution ought to be obeyed
testPool.modelAnswer: The Grundnorm is a presupposed, unenacted norm that legal science must assume in order to treat the historically first constitution — and everything validly created under it — as legally binding.

testPool.prompt: Name the term Kelsen (with Merkl) uses for the stepped hierarchy in which each level of norms derives its validity from the level above it.
testPool.modelAnswer: The Stufenbau — the stepped construction of norms, each deriving its validity from the norm above it, terminating in the Grundnorm.

testPool.prompt: Does Kelsen ground the Grundnorm's authority in morality (that the constitution is just) or in a purely formal presupposition needed for legal science?
options: In morality — the Grundnorm certifies the constitution as just
In a purely formal presupposition — it makes no moral claim at all

testPool.prompt: Which of the following best captures what Kelsen means by a 'pure' theory of law?
options: A theory that shows the legal system is morally sound and free of injustice
A theory purified of sociological, political and moral content, addressing only the question of normative validity
A theory that applies only to systems with a single, unbroken constitutional history
testPool.trapExplanation: The first option is the natural-law reading, not Kelsen's — 'pure' has nothing to do with moral soundness. The third invents a restriction Kelsen never states; the pure theory is offered as a general theory of any legal system.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that Kelsen's Grundnorm is an empirical fact you could confirm by observing what officials actually do, in the way Hart's rule of recognition can be?
sliderLabels: Confident — it is empirical, like the rule of recognition
Confident — it is a presupposition, not an empirical fact
testPool.explanation: The Grundnorm is a logical presupposition required to treat a constitution as binding — this is precisely the contrast this lesson draws with Hart's rule of recognition, which is an empirical fact about official practice.

testPool.prompt: Order these from the most concrete individual norm to the most foundational presupposed norm.
items: A court's judgment applying a statute to a dispute
A regulation made under delegated statutory authority
A statute enacted under the constitution

testPool.prompt: In this paraphrase of Kelsen's account of the basic norm, highlight the sentence that states the Grundnorm is not itself validated by any further, higher norm.
testPool.passage: Every norm's validity is traced back to a higher norm that authorised its creation. This chain cannot regress forever. The basic norm is therefore not validated by a further norm at all, but is simply presupposed as the necessary starting point from which the validity of everything else in the system is derived.
testPool.ratioSentence: The basic norm is therefore not validated by a further norm at all, but is simply presupposed as the necessary starting point from which the validity of everything else in the system is derived.

testPool.prompt: Kelsen formulates the basic norm roughly as: 'one ought to behave as the historically first constitution, and the norms created in accordance with it, prescribe.' Which word in that formula signals that the basic norm is hypothetical rather than a factual description?
testPool.explanation: 'Ought' marks the formula as normative rather than descriptive — it is prescribing that the constitution be treated as binding, not describing a fact about the world, which is exactly the is/ought separation the pure theory insists on.

testPool.prompt: A written constitution empowers a legislature to make statutes; a statute empowers a minister to make regulations; a regulation empowers a tribunal to decide individual disputes. Under Stufenbau reasoning, if the constitution were repealed and replaced with a validly authorised new one, what happens to the statute made under the old constitution?
options: It remains automatically valid regardless of the new constitution's terms
Its continued validity depends on whether the new constitution (directly or via transitional provisions) authorises it to continue
It becomes void the instant the old constitution is repealed, with no exceptions
testPool.explanation: Validity flows downward through the hierarchy from whichever constitution is currently presupposed as valid — a statute's continued validity depends on authorisation from the new constitution, typically through transitional or saving provisions, not on some free-standing validity of its own.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that, on Kelsen's theory, would justify legal science in presupposing a new Grundnorm for this government.
testPool.scenarioText: A military council seizes the presidential palace overnight. Six months later, its decrees are being enforced by functioning courts across the whole territory, taxes are collected under its authority, and no rival government controls any part of the country.
tappableSpans: its decrees are being enforced by functioning courts across the whole territory
taxes are collected under its authority
no rival government controls any part of the country
testPool.correctSpan: its decrees are being enforced by functioning courts across the whole territory
testPool.feedbackCorrect: That's the efficacy Kelsen requires — general, ongoing enforcement and compliance across the territory, not the initial seizure of power itself.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for evidence of lasting, general compliance rather than the moment force was used. Seizing a building is not efficacy; functioning courts enforcing the new order nationwide is.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that shows why no new Grundnorm should be presupposed in this scenario.
testPool.scenarioText: A group storms the state broadcaster and declares itself the new government. Within three days loyalist forces retake the building, the original ministers resume their posts, and the courts continue applying the pre-existing constitution exactly as before.
tappableSpans: the courts continue applying the pre-existing constitution exactly as before
testPool.correctSpan: the courts continue applying the pre-existing constitution exactly as before
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right — continued application of the old constitution shows the coup never achieved general efficacy, so the old Grundnorm remains presupposed throughout.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: The declaration of a new government is not enough on its own. Look for what the courts actually do afterwards — continuing to apply the old constitution shows the attempted new order never became efficacious.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario better illustrates a distinctly Kelsenian, rather than Hartian, way of explaining a legal system's ultimate validity?
testPool.scenarioA: A scholar explains that a constitution is binding because it is possible, and necessary for legal science, to presuppose a basic norm requiring obedience to it — without making any claim about what any official actually believes.
testPool.scenarioB: A scholar explains that a constitution is binding because the country's judges, as a matter of observable practice, accept and apply it as the ultimate criterion of legal validity from the internal point of view.
testPool.explanation: A is Kelsenian: validity rests on a presupposition required by legal science, independent of anyone's actual beliefs. B is Hartian: validity rests on an empirical social fact about what officials actually do and accept.

testPool.prompt: A country's constitution authorises a tax statute, which authorises a set of regulations, under which a tribunal fines a taxpayer. A student argues the tribunal's decision is 'purely factual' and has nothing to do with the Grundnorm. On Kelsen's theory, is the student right?
options: Yes — individual decisions like a tribunal's fine sit entirely outside the hierarchy of validity
No — the fine is an individual norm whose validity ultimately traces, through the regulation, the statute and the constitution, back to the presupposed Grundnorm
No — but only because tax law is a special case Kelsen exempts from the ordinary hierarchy
testPool.explanation: On the Stufenbau, every norm in the system — including a tribunal's individual decision — derives its validity from the norm above it, all the way up to the presupposed Grundnorm. Nothing in the hierarchy sits 'outside' it, and tax law gets no special exemption.

testPool.prompt: A rebel movement seizes control of a country's capital and declares a new constitution. Fourteen months later, its courts function nationwide, its currency and tax system are operating without rival, and the previous government has no effective presence anywhere in the territory. Analyse, using Kelsen's pure theory, whether legal science should now presuppose a new Grundnorm for this state.
factsToOrder: The rebel movement seizes the capital and declares a new constitution
Its courts function nationwide and its currency/tax system operates without rival
The previous government has no effective presence anywhere in the territory

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether legal science should presuppose a new Grundnorm for the order established by the rebel movement.
modelAnswer.rule: On Kelsen's pure theory, a new Grundnorm may be presupposed only once a new constitutional order achieves general, lasting efficacy — ongoing, widespread compliance and enforcement, not merely the initial seizure of power.
modelAnswer.application: The declaration of a new constitution alone would not be enough. But fourteen months of nationwide functioning courts, an operating currency and tax system, and the total absence of any effective rival government together show the general efficacy Kelsen's theory requires — this is not a fleeting or contested seizure of power.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Legal science should presuppose a new Grundnorm: the new order has become sufficiently efficacious to be treated, from this point, as the valid foundation of the legal system.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating the Grundnorm as if it were an enacted rule with an author, or assuming it changes the instant force is used rather than once a new order is genuinely efficacious. The second most common mistake is collapsing Kelsen into Hart because both are 'positivists' — the lesson exists to keep that difference precise.
